iOS for Android developers · Puzzle 3 · 4 of 5

The main actor

In puzzle 2, you moved work between queues by hand. Kotlin did the same job with coroutines and withContext. Swift has its own version, with one idea Kotlin doesn't have built in.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 2: Queues, not handlers

    Grand Central Dispatch runs tasks from dispatch queues on a pool of threads it manages. A serial queue runs one task at a time, in order; a concurrent queue can run several at once. The main queue runs on the main thread, so DispatchQueue.main.async is iOS's handler.post.

The problem

In puzzle 2, the image went to a background queue and back to the main queue, by hand, in nested blocks. In Kotlin you'd write it straight down, wrapping the slow part in withContext(Dispatchers.IO), and the coroutine does the hopping. Does Swift have that, and how does it keep screen work on the main thread?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Swift's version of a suspend function is an async function. Where it waits, you write await: at that point the function may give up its thread so other work can run on it, and later it resumes, possibly on a different thread. Like a coroutine, it reads straight down.

A task is one piece of async work running, like a coroutine. Swift adds one block Kotlin doesn't have built into the language: the actor. An actor is an object that lets only one task at a time touch its data; other code that wants in has to await its turn. That rules out two threads changing the same data at once, by construction rather than by remembering to lock. One catch: "one at a time" holds between awaits. When code on an actor reaches an await, it steps out, another task may come in and change the data, and when the first resumes, things may have moved on. So check your assumptions again after an await.

The most important one is the main actor. It protects all the data used to show the UI: code marked @MainActor always runs on the main thread, taking turns with rendering and touch handling. It's Swift's Dispatchers.Main. Note that await itself moves nothing: it frees the thread while waiting. Where loadUser()'s own work runs depends on which actor it belongs to, so heavy work still needs to be put off the main actor on purpose:

@MainActor
func showProfile() async {
    let user = await api.loadUser()   // the main thread is free while this waits
    nameLabel.text = user.name        // back on the main actor: safe to touch the screen
}

The analogy

The clerk again. An async function steps away from the desk while it waits for a reply, so the clerk can serve others. An actor is a room with one chair: only one task sits in it at a time; the rest wait at the door. Whoever steps out to wait for something gives up the chair, and may find things moved when they come back. The main actor is the clerk's own office, where all screen work happens.

Check yourself

Inside a @MainActor function, you await a network call that takes 2 seconds. Does the screen freeze?

Right. await gives the thread back while waiting.

Not quite. No manual queue is needed: await already lets the main thread go.

Not quite. At an await, the function gives up its thread; the main thread keeps handling touches.

Why can't two tasks change an actor's data at the same moment?

Not quite. Only the main actor is tied to the main thread; others run anywhere, still one task at a time.

Right. One task inside at a time.

What's the difference between the main actor and the main queue from puzzle 2?

Not quite. The main actor runs on the main thread: that's what makes UI work safe.

Right. Two ways of saying "on the main thread".

Not quite. The main actor protects UI data, and its code runs on the main thread.

Sources

  • The Swift Programming Language: Concurrency ("An asynchronous function in Swift can give up the thread that it's running on, which lets another asynchronous function run on that thread while the first function is blocked"; "actors allow only one task to access their mutable state at a time"; "the main actor protects all of the data that's used to show the UI. The main actor takes turns rendering the UI, handling UI events, and running code that you write that needs to query or update the UI")

What you now know

An async function can give up its thread while it waits, at each await: Swift's suspend. An actor lets only one task at a time touch its data. The main actor protects all UI data, so code marked @MainActor runs on the main thread: Swift's Dispatchers.Main.
